newsitem.title: RUSSIA: DeBakey arrives in Moscow for Yeltsin op.
newsitem.headline: DeBakey arrives in Moscow for Yeltsin op.

text.p: U.S. heart surgery expert Michael DeBakey returned to Moscow on Sunday to advise doctors treating President Boris Yeltsin, who was said by his wife to be optimistic and cracking jokes during his countdown to a bypass operation.

Russian officials whisked DeBakey away from Sheremetevo airport when he arrived on a flight from Amsterdam. Reporters and camera crews waited in vain outside the airport's VIP exit for a glimpse of him.

DeBakey, 88, said before leaving Houston on Saturday the heart bypass surgery, a procedure he pioneered in 1964, was expected "early next week", but he could not be more specific because of restrictions imposed by Russian officials.
He said he and three other Houston experts were only as consultants for the operation, which would involve multiple bypass surgery to improve bloodflow to Yeltsin's heart.
"We're not going to be a part of the operation. The Russian team is doing the operation, always has been. We're consultants," he said.
Russian cardiologist Renat Akchurin, who trained under DeBakey at Houston's Baylor College of Medicine, will perform the operation, expected to last between six and eight hours.
Hospital officials in Houston said DeBakey would be accompanied to Moscow by pathologist David Yawn, haematologist Clarence Alfrey and cardiovascular surgeon George Noon.
Yeltsin's wife Naina said in a television interview broadcast late on Saturday that her 65-year-old husband was cracking jokes with his doctors.

"Of course he is worried, but he is outwardly calm. He has a good contact with his doctors. I hear humour and jokes," she said, adding that many people were writing in with recipes for traditional medicines to make him better.
"He has optimism in his eyes. As always when he has decided something he believes it will turn out all right," she said.

But she said the family were keeping from him news reports "which we think he should not see". She gave as an example newspaper attacks on his daughter Tatyana accusing her of bringing documents for her father to sign.

DeBakey has said Yeltsin has been treated for anaemia and thyroid problems and now appeared to be ready for surgery. The Russian surgeons have been less forthcoming and officials have appeared uneasy about the American's openness.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, the Western leader closest to Yeltsin, made a brief stopover in Moscow on Saturday for talks with Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and passed on his good wishes.
"In these coming days we wish Boris Yeltsin all the best," Kohl told journalists after meeting Chernomyrdin for an hour.
Yeltsin's health is a subject of serious concern for Western governments and for investors worried about political stability.
Russian officials have been trying to project an atmosphere of business as usual despite tension in the armed forces over unpaid wages and uncertainty over Chechnya.
Businessman Boris Berezovsky, named this week as deputy secretary of the Kremlin's Security Council amid protests from the opposition, met Chechen representatives on Saturday.

Russian media reports indicated the talks in neigbouring Ingushetia with representatives of the separatist-dominated Chechen coalition government went well, although political issues were not on the agenda.
Radio Russia said Berezovsky would travel by car on Sunday to the Chechen capital Grozny for more talks aimed at paving the way for a meeting between separatist leaders and Chernomyrdin.
The Chechens have been concerned that peace efforts may collapse following the sacking last month by Yeltsin of Alexander Lebed, who negotiated agreements with the separatists.
